The preliminary findings reveal that the crew recognized the landing trajectory was compromised, prompting an immediate effort to abort the descent and regain altitude; however, the aircraft failed to clear the ground obstacles in time. This incident has triggered a rigorous investigation by aviation authorities to determine the precise sequence of mechanical, environmental, or human factors that led to the loss of control. As the National Transportation Safety Board continues its forensic analysis of the flight recorders and cockpit communications, the aviation industry faces renewed scrutiny regarding safety protocols for cargo operations and the management of unstable approaches during critical landing phases. This tragedy highlights critical vulnerabilities in airport ground safety and cargo flight protocols, likely necessitating stricter regulatory oversight regarding unstable approach procedures and runway proximity management. The outcome of this investigation will likely influence future pilot training standards and operational safety mandates for commercial logistics fleets operating in high-traffic urban environments.

primary_source.headline: Why this month's Microsoft patch release is a doozy
primary_source.content:
Microsoft’s patch for September is a doozy, with a record number of roughly 972 vulnerabilities fixed and 112 of them meeting the high critical-severity threshold.
It was only two months ago that Microsoft patched a then-record 570 vulnerabilities. Then, last month, Microsoft patched some 620 of them. Google and other companies have also published record numbers of vulnerabilities in recent months. Two weeks ago, OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon Web Services, Google, Microsoft, and 100 companies and organizations published an open letter warning of a narrowing window for patching vulnerabilities ahead of an expected tsunami of AI-enabled attacks that actively exploit them first. The industry is taking the threat seriously by pumping out unprecedented numbers of patches in their software.
Welcome to the new normal
Dustin Childs, a researcher at the Zero Day Initiative, calls the spikes the “new normal” and also cautions that despite them, the damage that’s likely to result from AI-assisted attacks could eventually be substantial.Read full article

primary_source.headline: Group of bipartisan lawmakers ask US government to ban several hack-for-hire firms
primary_source.content: A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers has asked the U.S. government to ban several hack-for-hire firms — companies that carry out cyberattacks on behalf of paying clients. The lawmakers accuse the firms of targeting Americans and abusing foreign courts to silence U.S. reporting on their activities. The list effectively bars U.S. businesses from transacting with a named entity, with the aim of restricting the companies from accessing critical technology needed to function, including software licenses and cloud infrastructure. The lawmakers say that these mercenary hacking companies have stolen data from thousands of Americans, and accuse the hackers of an “aggressive censorship campaign” to suppress public awareness of their alleged activities. “This coordinated effort effectively allows foreign entities to use foreign courts to keep the American public in the dark about cyber threats to their own country and undermines the fundamental constitutional rights of U.S. citizens,” the lawmakers said. It’s not clear if the Commerce Department will add the companies to its entity list, and a spokesperson did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment. The lawmakers’ letter said that the hack-for-hire companies “operated at the behest of the Qatari government” and that their targets included a former senior Republican lawmaker.

If successful, it establishes a powerful precedent for curbing the weaponization of foreign legal systems against U.S. investigative journalism and national security interests.

primary_source.content: Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordable• Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereIn August 2009, at the very first Gamescom expo, I sat in a small meeting room in Germany and played Mario Kart and World of Warcraft on a laptop, via technology that was then completely new: cloud gaming. It was a demonstration for a yet-to-be-launched service called Gaikai that promised to let you play any game in a browser window, without a console. (Here is an ancient video of that demonstration, featuring a very young Keza.) With a single click I could launch into any game, hosted on servers hundreds of miles away. It really did look like the future.Since then, plenty of companies have tried to be the first to truly crack game streaming, vying to be the Netflix of games. Sony ended up buying Gaikai for $380m (£242m) in 2012; its technology now powers the streamable classic games library on PlayStation, and the PS5’s advanced game streaming. OnLive, Gaikai’s first competitor, launched in 2011 but shut down after less than a year, leaving Sony to acquire all its patents. Google’s Stadia cloud gaming service also imploded, launching in 2019 and shutting down three years later. Continue reading...

sources.headline: Streaming from the cloud was meant to change games forever – what happened?

stories.brief: Cloud gaming, once heralded as the transformative future of interactive entertainment, has faced a turbulent trajectory characterized by high ambitions and significant operational hurdles. Initially popularized by pioneers like Gaikai and OnLive in the late 2000s, the technology promised to democratize high-end gaming by eliminating the need for expensive local hardware through browser-based streaming. Despite this potential, industry giants including Google, Sony, and Microsoft have struggled to achieve a seamless, affordable, and universally accessible experience, leading to notable failures like the shutdown of Google Stadia. While Sony successfully integrated Gaikai’s infrastructure into its PlayStation ecosystem, the broader dream of a "Netflix for games" remains elusive due to persistent latency issues and complex infrastructure demands. This history illustrates the profound gap between the technical demonstration of cloud streaming and the practical, scalable reality required to sustain a viable consumer market in the competitive gaming landscape. The persistent struggle to perfect cloud gaming highlights the fundamental limitations of current network infrastructure and the difficulty of replicating the low-latency responsiveness required for high-fidelity gaming. This ongoing challenge forces major tech conglomerates to pivot their strategies, shifting focus from pure cloud-native platforms toward hybrid models that prioritize local hardware performance over remote execution.

primary_source.headline: TDP Version 3.0: TDP hosts corporate workshops for its top leaders
primary_source.content: Hyderabad: Politics as service delivery, treating every citizen as a customer, party cadre as employees, and service delivery as the product, these were the corporate lessons the ruling TDP imparted to its top leaders, MPs, MLAs and cabinet ministers at a recent leadership conclave.In what was likely a first for south India, TDP conducted a corporate-style leadership conclave over two days on September 7 and 8 to share this thinking.Held at the TDP Central Office in Mangalagiri, the conclave was designed as a professional, interactive workshop to upskill elected representatives, strengthen leadership capabilities, and prepare the organisation for the upcoming local body elections and the 2029 general elections. Going beyond a conventional political conference, senior leaders themselves prepared and delivered sessions on political, organisational, governance, welfare and development issues.Participants were encouraged to raise questions, discuss practical challenges, and engage in detailed two-way discussions with the senior leadership."We should treat every citizen as a customer, cadre as employees, and service delivery as the product. Leaders must adapt to the generational shift and rapid growth of AI, using technology to improve political and administrative work. Actively engage SHG women and youth, promote DWCRA loans, and make participation in skill-development programmes mandatory," said Union Minister Chandrasekhar Pemmasani, who led one of the sessions for party leaders.Ten sessions were held over the two days, September 7 and 8, with Union Ministers Chandrasekhar Pemmasani and K Ram Mohan Naidu among those who took sessions. "The Telugu Desam Party has always been ahead in understanding the aspirations of the youth. Our approach must evolve in a way that enables us to understand the thinking of Gen Z," said Ram Mohan Naidu.Chief Minister and TDP National President N Chandrababu Naidu, addressing the conclave, said the focus must be on building effective leadership at every level and maintaining a continuous connection with the people.He directed party representatives to make victory in the forthcoming local body elections an immediate priority while simultaneously preparing for the 2029 elections. He stressed alliance unity, stronger grassroots engagement and coordination among leaders.The Chief Minister asked MLAs to set clear targets and identify 25 priority areas in every constituency, noting that focused work on these issues would help public representatives build recognition and credibility among the people.Coalition partners TDP and Jana Sena fire salvo against each other on social media ahead of local pollsHe also announced that leadership conclaves of this nature would be held once every three months, with MLAs who implement successful best practices given the opportunity to present them at subsequent meetings."Every ten years, a new generation emerges. Our performance and approach must change according to the changing generation," he said, stressing the need to understand the expectations of today's youth.On the second day, TDP National Working President Nara Lokesh addressed a session on "Political Communication and Public Orientation," stressing the need for elected representatives to take social media seriously and use it effectively to communicate directly with the public.He urged leaders to actively showcase the government's development and welfare initiatives through social media and to promptly counter Opposition misinformation with facts and evidence. Referring to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's use of selfie videos, Lokesh said leaders should adopt more direct and accessible forms of communication, citing his own use of selfie videos on the Suzlon wind projects and in countering the DSC misinformation campaign.Calling this "TDP Version 3.0," Lokesh said the party must come first, internal discussions and debate were encouraged, but the final word on the agenda would rest with Chandrababu Naidu and the party. He stressed stronger booth-level engagement, continuous cadre activation, direct public interaction, and faster resolution of people's issues.Lokesh said the party's biggest challenge was not delivery itself but its failure to communicate the truth as strongly and consistently as the Opposition communicates misinformation. He urged leaders to identify their weaknesses, work on them, and take responsibility for resolving public issues rather than merely forwarding them to higher leadership."This first-of-its-kind conclave marks a shift from conventional political meetings towards a structured leadership-development model combining training, peer learning, senior leadership mentorship and practical problem-solving, with a focus on building a more responsive, people-centric and election-ready organisation," said a senior TDP leader.

primary_source.content: Andrew Garfield’s charisma can’t save Paul Greengrass’s grim and depressingly generic period pieceHollywood loves giving young actors their own historical epic as much as audiences seem to dislike watching them. Timothée Chalamet and Chris Pine’s least remembered roles are in the medieval set films The King and Outlaw King (no relation), Ridley Scott’s The Last Duel made back only a third of its $100m budget and earlier this year, the Saudi-backed seventh-century drama Desert Warrior starring Anthony Mackie and Ben Kingsley quietly became one of the biggest flops of all time. Last week, it was reported that Scott blamed the failure of Gladiator II on Paul Mescal not being “masculine enough” in a logical leap which only makes sense if your barometer for masculinity is a man who throws hotel phones and yells at producers in storage closets.On paper, The Uprising should be different: it’s a historical epic from a blue-chip director (the Bourne trilogy’s Paul Greengrass), a nuanced, introspective leading man (Andrew Garfield) and a milieu that uncomfortably chimes with the western world’s backslide into repressive authoritarianism (The Peasants’ Revolt of 1381). In reality, it is a disjointed slog through the mud with the emotional depth of a History Channel rerun. Continue reading...

sources.headline: The Uprising review – the peasants are revolting in muddled historical epic

stories.brief: The Guardian’s review of Paul Greengrass’s latest film, The Uprising, characterizes the project as a disjointed and generic historical epic that fails to capitalize on its promising premise. Despite starring Andrew Garfield and tackling the politically resonant subject of the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt, the film is criticized for lacking emotional depth and narrative cohesion, ultimately resembling a tedious television documentary rather than a compelling cinematic experience. This critique arrives amidst a broader industry trend where high-budget historical epics—such as The King, The Last Duel, and Desert Warrior—have consistently struggled to find commercial success or critical acclaim. The review highlights a disconnect between Hollywood’s persistent investment in these period pieces and the audience's apparent lack of appetite for them, suggesting that even established directors like Greengrass are struggling to revitalize a genre that currently feels disconnected from contemporary viewer interests. The continued commercial and critical failure of high-budget historical epics signals a potential shift in studio investment strategies, suggesting that star power and prestige directors are no longer sufficient to guarantee the viability of the genre in a saturated market. This trend forces Hollywood to reevaluate the risk-to-reward ratio of period dramas, potentially leading to a contraction in production for these costly, large-scale historical projects.

sources.headline: What Should My Children Do? by Daniel Susskind review – the case for embracing tech in the classroom

stories.brief: Daniel Susskind’s latest work, "What Should My Children Do?", offers a compelling, optimistic counter-narrative to the prevailing anxiety surrounding artificial intelligence in modern education. By drawing a historical parallel to the 1979 Cockcroft report, which addressed widespread panic over the introduction of pocket calculators in classrooms, Susskind illustrates how society frequently mistakes technological integration for the erosion of fundamental cognitive skills. Just as critics once feared that calculators would create a generation of "dumbed-down drones" incapable of basic arithmetic, contemporary skeptics now view AI as a threat to essential learning processes. Susskind argues that rather than retreating from these innovations, educators and policymakers must embrace the transformative potential of AI to enhance pedagogical outcomes. His analysis serves as a crucial reminder that educational crises are often cyclical, and that the successful adoption of new tools depends less on prohibition and more on thoughtful, strategic integration into the curriculum. This perspective is vital because it shifts the educational debate from reactionary fear-mongering to proactive adaptation, ensuring that future generations are equipped to leverage AI as a cognitive force multiplier rather than being displaced by it. primary_source.content: Sometimes founders search high and low for the right startup idea, while other times it comes to them. Federico Felici and Jonas Buchli are two of the lucky ones. Over and over again, they heard the same thing from fusion companies: “We would ideally buy many of the components to make our our control system, but there isn’t really anybody providing them — and especially there isn’t anybody who speaks the language of fusion,” Felici told TechCrunch. For years, the two founders have worked to develop new ways to control experimental fusion devices. “We spent quite a lot of our time solving exactly the problems that our customers need to solve,” he said. “It felt like the right time.” Yet few companies specialize in the hardware and software required to control the fusion reactors themselves. “Across the industry, many companies make their own control systems from scratch,” Felici said. “But actually, 80% of each company’s control system is really exactly the same.” Fusion power plants generate electricity by harnessing the energy released when two atoms fuse, which is more likely to occur in a superheated plasma. But plasmas are fickle, and maintaining the proper temperature, shape, and fuel level requires split-second decision-making. The control systems used to maintain those conditions are complex to develop and deploy, but much of the fundamental physics is consistent across reactor designs. Fusionality plans to build off that commonality to develop a suite of control systems and simulation environments which startups can then fine-tune to work with their specific design.

This approach allows fusion developers to focus their resources on unique design challenges rather than reinventing fundamental control mechanisms. By commoditizing the underlying control infrastructure for fusion reactors, Fusionality could drastically lower barriers to entry and reduce development costs for the burgeoning fusion sector. This shift toward modular, standardized technology is essential for transitioning fusion energy from experimental physics projects into a scalable, reliable component of the global energy grid.

primary_source.headline: GOG brings back "big box" PC games, one printable template at a time
primary_source.content:
Those who remember PC gaming in the days before Steam may have fond memories of the "big box" packaging that made those games stand out as shelf eye candy and sought-after in-home collectibles. Today, PC gaming platform GOG is hoping to reignite some of the nostalgia for those days by adding downloadable 3D models and printable, foldable high-res packaging scans for a handful of PC games on the platform.
Thus far, the "Printable Big Box" collection on GOG is limited to just five games: Armikrog, Descent, Hitman: Codename 47, Myst, and Star Trek: 25th Anniversary. Players browsing those games on the GOG store will now see "3D Boxes" listed among the included "Goodies" before purchase. Owners of those games on GOG can download a ZIP file containing a version of the box art as an animated 3D object file (in an easy-to-open GLB format) and a "flat printable template" in PDF, SVG, and Adobe Illustrator formats. Those downloads allow for what GOG calls "a proper papercraft project for anyone who misses shelves full of PC game boxes."

      The 3D model animates to show the front flap opening.
        Credit:
          GOG
      
"Physical media doesn’t survive the way software can—boxes get lost, crushed, thrown out," GOG writes in today's announcement. "Scanning them, and letting you print your own, is preservation in a different shape: the same mission that keeps these games running on modern PCs, applied to the objects they used to come in."Read full article

stories.brief: The open-source project Geiger, recently introduced on Hacker News by Atomburst, addresses the growing security concerns surrounding local AI agent execution by providing a critical visibility layer for machine-level AI activity. As developers increasingly integrate autonomous agents into local environments, the risk of unauthorized file access or system manipulation has escalated, necessitating robust oversight tools. Geiger functions as a monitoring utility that maps out every active AI agent on a user's machine, explicitly detailing the specific files, directories, and system resources each agent can access or modify. By offering this granular transparency, the tool empowers developers to audit agent behavior, identify potential security vulnerabilities, and enforce stricter permission boundaries before deployment. This release reflects a broader industry shift toward AI observability, where the focus is moving from merely running models to securing the complex, often opaque interactions between agents and local operating systems. As AI agents gain deeper integration into local workflows, tools like Geiger are essential for preventing agent-based malware or accidental data exfiltration, effectively establishing a necessary baseline for local AI security and governance.

This shift in consumer behavior signals a potential long-term erosion of traditional investment and savings models, which could destabilize economic growth and retirement systems if younger generations abandon long-term financial planning. Understanding these trends is critical for policymakers and financial institutions attempting to address the growing disconnect between institutional economic structures and the lived realities of the emerging workforce.

primary_source.content: Instacart is the latest app to bake a conversational AI assistant into its platform. The company announced on Wednesday that it’s launching a new AI-powered grocery shopping assistant called Clementine that can turn a conversation, grocery list, or recipe into a ready-to-buy cart. With Clementine, users can decide what to make for dinner, simplify grocery shopping, and stay on budget, the company says. For example, users can ask the assistant queries like, “I need a week of budget-friendly kids’ lunches,” “high-protein, easy dinners for two,” or “order my usuals.” The launch of the AI assistants indicates that delivery apps no longer just want to be places where people find and buy groceries, but also where they make decisions before a purchase. These platforms are now competing not only on delivery speed and variety, but also on becoming the default planning tool for households when it comes to grocery shopping. Additionally, they’re looking to keep users in their own apps for grocery and meal planning, rather than having them turn to popular AI chatbots like ChatGPT. Instacart says Clementine can generate personalized recipes or surface ones from trusted publishers. It also tailors recommendations to each household’s preferences, including dietary needs such as gluten-free, vegetarian, nut-free, or organic options. The AI assistant will also surface relevant deals and promotions while suggesting lower-cost alternatives. Additionally, users can upload a photo of a handwritten grocery list or a screenshot of a digital one, and Clementine can turn it into a cart. “Every night, millions of families ask the same question: ‘What’s for dinner?’ Not knowing the answer, let alone what to shop for, is one of the most universal human experiences, and a problem Instacart is built to solve,” said Chris Rogers, CEO of Instacart, in an emailed press release. “We’ve spent nearly 15 years learning how families shop and eat, and Clementine puts that knowledge to work.”

primary_source.content:
Leading chipmakers Samsung Electronics and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. announced plans to adopt ASML’s latest chipmaking machines in the next several years—and they also joined Intel in agreeing to a crucial technology change that could boost chip production on the new machines by 40 percent.
This signifies the semiconductor industry’s broader embrace of high NA EUV photolithography technology that can cost up to $400 million per machine and is only provided by the Dutch technology company ASML, Bloomberg reports. The technology would allow chip designers to implement even smaller features in potentially more powerful and efficient next-generation chips produced for AI data centers and consumer electronics such as smartphones, tablets, and laptops.
ASML’s EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography machines enable chipmakers to use powerful laser light to imprint patterns in silicon wafers, layer by layer, and gradually form the computer circuitry that makes silicon chips work. Compared to older deep ultraviolet lithography, EUV technology harnesses a more powerful source of light with a shorter wavelength to create even smaller features on silicon wafers.Read full article

primary_source.headline: Update to Google’s AI weather model improves forecast accuracy
primary_source.content:
Google is one of the major players in AI (meaning machine learning) weather forecast model space. The models it and others generate have their strengths and weaknesses, but the main advantage is that they can have forecast performance similar to traditional models while requiring far less computing horsepower to run. That means they can be run more frequently.
Google recently released version 3 of its WeatherNext model, with the biggest change being that it now ingests some satellite weather data, shortening the lag time between current weather conditions and generating a new forecast. The update is detailed in a white paper.
Reanalysis
Many weather models make use of what’s called a “reanalysis,” which is a sort of model of its own. Reanalyses take in all kinds of weather data and combine them into a single, consistent global snapshot of the atmosphere. That requires that they provide estimates for conditions over locations without real-world measurements, because weather forecast models need to work with a global picture.Read full article

This controversy underscores the urgent need for standardized, independent auditing of frontier AI models to prevent the erosion of scientific trust.
